segments.text: Episode eighty-seven. Next stop... a ring of fire.
Tomorrow, February sixth, the Moon will pass in front of the Sun. But it won't cover it completely.
segments.headline: Tomorrow: an eclipse

segments.text: A blazing ring of sunlight will surround the dark Moon. It's called an annular eclipse, or a ring of fire.
segments.headline: A ring of fire

segments.text: Why a ring? Because the Moon's orbit is an oval. Tomorrow it's far from Earth, so it looks slightly too small to cover the Sun.
segments.headline: The Moon looks too small

segments.text: The ring will be visible along a path across southern Chile and Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil, then across the Atlantic to Africa.
segments.headline: Where to see it

segments.text: Near its maximum, the ring lasts up to about seven minutes and fifty-one seconds. Unusually long.

visual.label: of ring of fire, at most

segments.text: Here's a fun coincidence: the Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but also about four hundred times farther away. That's why they look the same size.
segments.headline: A perfect coincidence

segments.text: Most important: never look at it without certified eclipse glasses. Even a ring of sunlight can damage your eyes.
segments.headline: Protect your eyes

segments.text: Not in the path? Many observatories will stream it live online.
segments.headline: Watch online

segments.text: Tomorrow, the Red Planet is about to be at its brightest in two years. Next stop: Mars. Follow, so you don't miss episode eighty-eight.
